title: What a mosque is
hookLine: the place of prostration, open for prayer, learning and gathering
last: BEFORE SLEEP — IN YOUR NAME I SLEEP.

lines: A DOME, A STRIP MALL, A BASEMENT.
A WEEK-LONG VISIT, STEP BY STEP.
cards: You've probably driven past one. Maybe a grand building with a dome and a tall minaret. Maybe a converted shop on a strip mall, with a hand-painted sign and a row of shoes visible through the glass door.
Maybe a room in a university basement. From the outside, they look nothing alike. And if you're not Muslim, you may never have been inside one, or been sure you'd be allowed.
This week, the path walks you through a visit, step by step, starting with the name on the sign. Today: what a mosque is.

teach.b: The Arabic word is masjid. You met its root on day one hundred five: sujud, prostration. A masjid is simply the place of prostration, where people put their foreheads on the floor.
Notice what the name doesn't require. Not a dome. Not a minaret.

teach.h: THE WHOLE EARTH IS A MASJID.
teach.b: Bukhari reports the Prophet ﷺ saying that the whole earth has been made a masjid for him, a place of prayer. That's why you'll see Muslims pray in parks, airports and parking lots; any clean ground will do.
So what makes a building a mosque? Go back to the first ones.

When the Prophet arrived in Medina, one of the first things he did was build one, with his own hands alongside the companions, as the reports describe: walls of mud brick, pillars of palm trunks, a roof of palm leaves.
Inside went the five prayers, of course. But also teaching. And poor companions with nowhere else to go, staying in a sheltered part of the mosque known as the Suffah.

Bukhari even reports a tent pitched in the mosque for a wounded companion, so the Prophet could visit him from close by, and, on an Eid, men from Abyssinia putting on a display with their spears while the Prophet's wife Aisha watched.
A house of prayer that was also a school, a shelter, a clinic and a town square.

teach.h: A PLACE TO BOW, AND MORE.
teach.b: Mosques today often carry on the same mix: the five prayers, weekend classes, food drives, weddings, funerals. And some hold open days for visitors who simply want to see.

how: Muslims gather at the mosque for the five daily prayers and Friday prayer, and for classes, community meals, weddings and funerals; many mosques also welcome visitors.

o: a market hall where traders meet after prayer
a domed building with a tall minaret beside it
a place of prostration, where foreheads touch the floor

games.q: what's inside the word masjid — tap the pairs.

s: a mosque must have a dome and a minaret
the name only means a place of prostration; some mosques are simple rooms.
the Prophet's mosque in Medina was also a shelter and a place of teaching
poor companions lived on the Suffah, and teaching happened there.
Muslims may only pray inside a mosque
Bukhari reports the whole earth was made a masjid: any clean ground will do.

games.q: you've just arrived in Medina after a long, dangerous journey, and a community is forming around you. what does the Prophet ﷺ set about building?
o: a mosque, with his own hands, of mud brick and palm trunks
games.why: one of the first things he did was build the mosque, working alongside the companions; it became school, shelter and square.

practice: Picture the ground you're on right now: the floor under your chair, the earth under the building. If the whole earth is a place to bow, this spot counts too. Let that settle for a few breaths, and feel the ground.

wordCard.voice: Masjid. A mosque: the place of prostration, open for prayer, learning and gathering. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the place of prostration, from sajada, to prostrate.

carryVoice: Your line: a place to bow. A park, a quiet corner, the floor of your room: any of them could be one. Day one hundred thirty-seven, done.
